weaknesses: The central evidence for catastrophic knowledge loss is questionable. The empirical scope is too narrow for the broad claims: one 3B model, one 3x3 task, one image domain, only 100 jigsaw test examples, and apparently one training seed. The perplexity evidence does not identify the proposed mechanism. It compares responses with different prompts, lengths, and structures; per-token perplexity can be dominated by generic reasoning text. The median-versus-lower-quartile statistic is arbitrary, lacks uncertainty testing, and low perplexity alone does not imply gradient compatibility with old tasks.

The theoretical interpretation overreaches. Theorem 5.2 is the generic local symmetry of a gradient inner product. It establishes neither the sign nor magnitude of interference and does not imply that reinforcing a low-perplexity response preserves prior knowledge over many nonlinear updates. The link from low perplexity to positive gradient alignment is unsupported, and the probability-sums-to-one argument is inapplicable across different input contexts.

Reproducibility and positioning are incomplete: reward-component aggregation, restart details, several optimization settings, seeds, and release artifacts are missing or ambiguous. weaknesses: The central causal claim that data distribution, rather than the algorithm, explains RFT's retention is not established. The proposed low-perplexity explanation is largely confounded and partly circular: samples generated by a model initialized from the base model and KL-regularized toward it will predictably have lower base-model perplexity than GPT-4o text. The theoretical argument does not support the claimed mechanism. The symmetry theorem is essentially symmetry of a first-order gradient inner product; low perplexity does not imply positive gradient alignment with prior examples or reduced negative interference. The LBK expression omits the learning-rate factor required by the preceding inequality, neglects the remainder when treating the ratio as a lower bound, and interprets large kernel norm as harmful even though its signed contraction can represent either positive transfer or interference. Stabilization of LBK also does not demonstrate eNTK stability.

Performance loss is repeatedly equated with loss of knowledge, although Figure 3 directly shows an output-format change. Parser-sensitive benchmark degradation, including near-zero scores, could reflect instruction or formatting collapse rather than erased semantic knowledge. Format-controlled evaluation, alternative prompting, rapid-relearning tests, or representation-level probes are needed to distinguish these explanations.

The novelty premise is weakly supported. Zero exact-match accuracy on only 100 nine-piece puzzles is expected even for a system performing substantially above random because there are 9! possible permutations, and it neither proves that the task is absent from pretraining nor that no relevant capability exists. The math and scientific-QA tasks are plainly not novel to the base models.

The evidence lacks repeated seeds, uncertainty estimates, and a described validation/model-selection protocol; the 100-example jigsaw test set is particularly small. Generality is also limited to the Qwen2.5 family and GRPO. Reproducibility is weakened by unreleased code and trajectories, incomplete training/evaluation details, an unspecified combination of the three rewards, and a contradictory description of image preprocessing as cropping in the main text but resizing in Algorithm 1.

The paper frequently equates benchmark-score loss with loss of prior knowledge. Figure 3 instead demonstrates output-format drift: the model still localizes an object but answers in the wrong schema. Statistical support and reproducibility are insufficient: the jigsaw test contains only 100 examples, no repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, and checkpoint-selection details are unclear. Novelty and scope are limited relative to the cited contemporaneous work already showing that online RL forgets less. The central empirical observation is useful: SFT on self-generated/RFT trajectories generally retains prior-task performance better than answer-only SFT or SFT on GPT-4o-generated trajectories.

Experiments cover two multimodal model sizes, two language-model sizes, three target-task settings, and a broad collection of retained-capability benchmarks; the reported hierarchy of forgetting is reasonably consistent and often has large effect sizes.

The appendices provide compute costs, prompts, learning curves, mixture ablations, alternative GRPO recipes, and an informative experiment showing that a shorter RFT phase can already yield useful SFT data.
weaknesses: The conclusion that data distribution, rather than the algorithm, explains RFT's retention is not causally established. RFT and SFT differ in learning rate, KL regularization, reward weighting and filtering, update count, and optimizer/reference-policy restarts. SFT on RFT rollouts shows that data matter, but does not show that algorithmic differences do not matter; indeed, RFT still retains substantially better than rollout-based SFT in several results.

The proposed mechanism is technically unconvincing. The symmetry theorem is essentially first-order symmetry of gradient inner products for a single-example SGD update, whereas the experiments use batches, sequences, Adam-like optimization, and GRPO. Low perplexity of a model's own sampled trajectories is expected by construction and does not imply favorable gradient direction or compatibility with arbitrary prior knowledge. Applying the local symmetry result retrospectively to the long pretraining trajectory is unjustified.

The LBK proxy is not shown to faithfully measure eNTK interference under the actual optimizer: it is derived after ignoring step-size and higher-order effects and is computed from the same likelihood changes that constitute the forgetting outcome. Consequently, the claimed magnitude-versus-direction decomposition is not independently validated.

Key controls are missing. The trajectory sources differ in length, style, correctness filtering, and difficulty, but there are no length- or update-norm-matched comparisons, low-perplexity filtering of GPT-4o trajectories, base-model rollouts paired with gold answers, or KL-regularized SFT baselines. These interventions are needed to distinguish base-model perplexity from simpler format, gradient-scale, and self-distillation effects.

Much of the extreme 'forgetting' may be output-format collapse rather than loss of knowledge: answer-only SFT repeatedly trains short lists of numbers, and the grounding example fails by switching from JSON to a numeric list. A format-matched no-reasoning control and evaluations that separate latent task competence from decoding-format compliance are absent. The qualitative jigsaw chains are also generic scene narratives rather than convincing assembly reasoning.

The statistical evidence is limited: results appear to be single runs without confidence intervals, the jigsaw test contains only 100 examples, and models are reported at different training steps without a stated validation/checkpoint-selection protocol. Zero exact-match accuracy over a 9! output space does not establish that the task was absent from pretraining.

Reproducibility remains incomplete because code is only promised and important details of rollout construction, reward aggregation, sampling, and LBK estimation are missing. The main text says images are cropped to divisible dimensions, whereas the appendix specifies bicubic resizing, and the limitations section is inconsistent with the added language-model experiments.

Shows a striking, consistent empirical pattern across Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B: RFT learns the jigsaw task while largely retaining prior benchmark performance, whereas conventional SFT can degrade it severely.

Training SFT on RFT-generated trajectories is an insightful intervention. The early-RFT self-generation result is especially useful, suggesting a practical way to obtain effective supervision without completing the very expensive RFT run.

Extensions to language-only math and scientific QA, along with Pareto curves, perplexity analyses, mixture controls, learning-rate sweeps, and compute reporting, substantially broaden the empirical study.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the learning-dynamics formulation provides a potentially useful vocabulary for separating update magnitude from cross-example alignment.
weaknesses: The central theoretical inference is not established. Theorem 5.2 is essentially symmetry of a first-order gradient inner product; low base-model perplexity does not imply positive gradient alignment with particular prior examples or low interference with them. Thus the PPL evidence is correlational and does not explain why RFT preserves prior knowledge.

The claimed catastrophic forgetting may partly be output-format or instruction-following interference rather than erased knowledge. Figure 3 explicitly shows grounding predictions changing from JSON to a numeric list, which can destroy exact-match scores. Format-robust evaluation, probing, or recovery experiments are needed to distinguish these effects.

The conclusion that data distribution, rather than algorithmic differences, is decisive is too strong. RFT and SFT differ in learning rate, batch construction, token and update budgets, KL regularization, trajectory length, and periodic restart policy. SFT on RFT rollouts shows that data matters, but does not rule out algorithmic contributions; KL-, token-, update-norm-, and parameter-distance-matched controls are absent.

The low-perplexity mechanism is not causally isolated. GRPO rollouts are low-perplexity by construction and also differ from GPT-4o trajectories in style, length, content, and correctness. Within-source PPL matching, controlled paraphrases, or low-PPL unrelated/self-generated controls would be more diagnostic. Several displayed chains of thought are generic, so a padding or contextualization effect remains plausible.

Statistical robustness is limited: the jigsaw test contains only 100 images, results appear to use single runs without confidence intervals, and all model experiments use the Qwen2.5 family at 3B/7B scale. Some target-task differences are therefore within plausible sampling or training variance, and cross-architecture generality is unknown.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the substantial compute requirement: the reward-component aggregation is unspecified, several training and checkpoint-selection details are missing, code is only promised, and the dataset description inconsistently specifies cropping versus resizing. The assertion that jigsaw solving is absent from pretraining is also stronger than the zero-shot evidence supports.

The most valuable experiment is training SFT on correct GRPO-generated trajectories. Its substantially better retention than answer-only and GPT-4o-trajectory SFT provides credible evidence that supervision data distribution matters, beyond the direct RFT-versus-SFT comparison.

The empirical pattern is replicated across two Qwen2.5-VL scales, numerous retained-capability benchmarks, language-model mathematics, and scientific QA. Learning-rate sweeps, Pareto curves, reasoning/non-reasoning mixtures, and the short-RFT self-generation experiment add useful breadth.

The paper transparently reports prompts, rewards, major hyperparameters, and unusually large compute costs. The exact-reward jigsaw task also supplies a convenient setting for studying acquisition of a weak initial capability.
weaknesses: The headline causal conclusion—data distribution rather than algorithmic differences explains RFT's retention—is not established. RFT includes explicit KL regularization while SFT does not, and the methods differ in learning rate, optimizer trajectory, token budget, reward weighting, and periodic optimizer/reference-policy resets. Essential controls include SFT with KL-to-base regularization and comparisons matched by target accuracy, update norm, token count, and model KL drift.

The supervised datasets are not controlled interventions on perplexity. GRPO trajectories are correctness-filtered (retaining roughly 65% of samples), while the compared datasets differ simultaneously in prompt difficulty, sample count, trajectory length, style, source model, and answer conditioning. Low perplexity is therefore correlated with many alternative explanations and is not independently manipulated.

The theoretical analysis does not justify the main mechanism. Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 are essentially the standard first-order gradient-inner-product identity and its symmetry. Symmetry does not imply that an example's low absolute perplexity entails positive alignment with prior-data gradients. Moreover, the unsigned LBK bound cannot distinguish beneficial transfer from destructive interference, and stability of this lower bound does not demonstrate stability of the eNTK. The claim that the kernel term is dominant is asserted rather than established.

The paper equates benchmark-score degradation with loss of prior knowledge, although Figure 3 explicitly shows a grounding failure caused by switching output format. Similar instruction- or formatting interference can severely depress exact-match scores without erasing semantic knowledge. Format-normalized or constrained decoding, likelihood-based retention measures, recoverability tests, and direct knowledge probes are needed before calling the effect catastrophic knowledge forgetting.

The jigsaw evidence is statistically narrow: only 100 test instances, apparently one run per condition, no confidence intervals or seed variation, and no out-of-distribution image sources, grid sizes, or model families. Zero exact-match accuracy on a 9! permutation problem does not establish that the task was absent from pretraining, particularly because jigsaws and COCO images are well known.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the promised code release: exact split identifiers, seeds, decoding/evaluation settings, GPT-4o version, and the construction and aggregation of LBK are insufficiently specified. There is also a dataset-construction inconsistency: Section 3 describes cropping excess pixels, whereas Algorithm 1 uses ceiling dimensions and bicubic resizing. Overall, the empirical observation is promising, but the causal and theoretical claims are stronger than the current evidence.
